parts.label: (a)
key_concepts: symmetrical charge distribution on spherical conductor
electric field lines normal to conducting surface
hints: Hint 1: Think about how charge spreads itself on an isolated sphere and what this symmetry means for the pattern of field lines just outside the surface.
Hint 2: Recall the rule for the direction of field lines at any conducting surface, then extend those lines backwards to see where they seem to meet.
parts.proper_answer: Field lines leave the sphere radially, normal to its surface. Extended backwards they all meet at the centre, identical to the field of a point charge at the centre.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Charge Spreads Uniformly on a Sphere**
Charge on an isolated spherical conductor repels itself and spreads evenly over the outer surface. The distribution has complete spherical symmetry, so there is no preferred direction except away from the centre.

Step 2: **Field Lines Must Leave Normally**
A key rule is that electric field lines are always perpendicular to the surface of a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium. For a sphere, the normal direction at every point is along the radius. So outside the sphere the lines are radial.

Step 3: **Lines Appear to Come From the Centre**
If you trace these radial lines backwards, they all intersect at the centre of the sphere. That is exactly the pattern for a point charge, so: $$\text{field outside sphere} = \text{field of point charge } q \text{ at centre}$$

parts.label: (b)(i)
key_concepts: electric field as negative potential gradient
hints: Hint 1: You are given a graph of $V$ against $x$ but asked for $E$. Focus on the curved section at $x = 6.0\text{ cm}$ and think about what the steepness of the graph there tells you.
Hint 2: Draw a tangent at $x = 6.0\text{ cm}$ and pick two widely spaced points on that straight tangent line to find $\Delta V / \Delta x$. Remember to convert $x$ to metres.
Hint 3: Take the magnitude of the gradient to get $E$, and check your value is near $10^5\text{ N C}^{-1}$ with correct units $\text{N C}^{-1}$ or $\text{V m}^{-1}$.
parts.proper_answer: $E = -$ gradient of $V$-$x$ graph at $x = 6.0\text{ cm} \approx 9.0 \times 10^{4}\text{ N C}^{-1}$ directed radially outward.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link $E$ to the Slope of $V$**
Field strength is the rate of change of potential with distance: $$E = -\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta x}$$ The minus sign just means $V$ falls in the direction of $E$. The magnitude is the steepness of the $V$-$x$ graph at that $x$.

Step 2: **Draw a Tangent at $x = 6.0\text{ cm}$**
At $x = 6.0\text{ cm}$, $V \approx 5.4 \times 10^{3}\text{ V}$. Lay a ruler to touch the curve only at that point. Read off two points on the tangent, for example $V_1 \approx 9.0 \times 10^{3}\text{ V}$ at $x_1 = 2.0\text{ cm}$ and $V_2 \approx 1.8 \times 10^{3}\text{ V}$ at $x_2 = 10.0\text{ cm}$.

Step 3: **Calculate the Magnitude**
Find the gradient magnitude: $$E = \left|\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta x}\right| = \frac{(9.0 - 1.8)\times 10^{3}}{(10.0 - 2.0)\times 10^{-2}}$$ $$E \approx \frac{7.2 \times 10^{3}}{0.080} \approx 9.0 \times 10^{4}\text{ N C}^{-1}$$ This is the field strength at $6.0\text{ cm}$ from the centre.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
key_concepts: constant potential inside hollow charged conductor
radius from flat section of V-x graph
hints: Hint 1: Look carefully at the left-hand end of Fig. 6.2 where the graph changes shape. Identify up to what value of $x$ the potential stays flat.
Hint 2: Recall what $E$ and $V$ must be inside a conductor in equilibrium, and link the flat part with zero gradient to the surface of the sphere.
parts.proper_answer: $R = 2.5\text{ cm}$. $V$ is constant at about $13 \times 10^{3}\text{ V}$ for $x$ less than $R$ because $E = 0$ inside a conductor, so no work is done moving charge inside.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot Where the Graph Stops Falling**
From $x = 0$ to about $x = 2.5\text{ cm}$ the graph in Fig. 6.2 is horizontal at $V \approx 13 \times 10^{3}\text{ V}$. Beyond that it curves down as $1/x$. The changeover marks the surface, so: $$R \approx 2.5\text{ cm}$$

Step 2: **Why Potential Is Flat Inside**
Inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium free charges would move if there were any field, so: $$E = 0 \text{ inside}$$ Since $E = -dV/dx$, zero field means zero gradient, so $V$ stays constant and equal to the surface potential throughout the interior.
